utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let the Registrar call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case Number IT-99-37-PT, the Prosecutor versus Milan Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Christina Romano, and here with me the Prosecutor, Carla del Ponte, and Milbert Shin, and Susan Grogan as our case manager. And Mr. Shin will be doing most of the arguments today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: For the defendant Milan Milutinovic, I appear, John Livingston, together with Mr. Radoje Stefanovic. There's also other counsel from Serbia here. I have an application in relation to him. I don't know whether Your Honours would wish to hear that in private session or in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're in open session, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: The position is that Mr. Milutinovic wishes Mr. Papic to be present in court. He's currently unassigned in this case. He wouldn't therefore normally have any right to be in court. He has, however, as Your Honours will be aware from the paperwork, have some association with the work that's been done in this case so far. It is intended that he will be a legal assistant in the case in the future. And although again that wouldn't qualify him to be in court, I would ask that on this one occasion bearing in mind that he is here, that Your Honours will allow him to sit in court and listen to all the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll grant the application. However, since he has not been assigned, there will be no right of audience, and no right of course of any remuneration for this hearing. Yes, Mr. Caric.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, distinguished member of the Trial Chamber, my name is Slavoljub Caric, the consul of the embassy of Serbia and Montenegro, and I'll present the explanation -- the explanation of the guarantees for provisional release of Mr. Milan Milutinovic. Just one correction concerning the translation, I am the counsellor, not consul. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Livingston, it's your application.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] It is.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, it is. Your Honour, before I begin, let me indicate that although the word confidential appears on all the filings in this case, except bar one, I am -- I hope this was conveyed to Your Honours -- I am content that the vast bulk of this motion be dealt with in open session. But there are three particular matters which I would ask Your Honour to hear me on in private session, which we would like not to be dealt with in public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, well if you indicate when it is you wish to go into private session, the confidential matters, the Chamber will no doubt go into that session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honour, I think it might be easiest if I deal with those matters straight away and get them out of the way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We shall have to have an adjournment as usual, at 4.00, time for the interpreters' adjournment. We can't sit much at all beyond 5.00, so time is limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: I don't expect that I shall be too long. I think I can put my submissions quite succinctly I hope without any detriment to their strength.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the starting point, of course, for any provisional release application is Rule 65. And there are, in essence, two criteria which that particular rule - it's Rule 65(B) - is concerned with. It says that "Release may be ordered by a Trial Chamber only after giving the host country and the state to which the accused seeks to be released the opportunity to be heard." And I think just pausing there, neither of those countries raise any problem about the provisional release of this defendant. It goes on to say, and this is the critical matter for this Chamber: "If it is satisfied that the accused will appear for trial," that's the first point, "and if released will pose -- will not pose a danger to any victim, witness, or other person." Dealing with the first point, that is the -- whether the accused will appear for trial, in my submission, at the bottom of that particular issue is this question about whether the surrender was voluntary or not. And in my submission, it's a distinguishing factor which marks off this defendant from his coaccused in this trial, because the Appeals Chamber, as this Chamber will be aware, found that neither the surrender of General Ojdanic nor the surrender of Nikola Sainovic were voluntary. Your Honour, the points in favour of this defendant are these, and they are made out in my submission very clearly in the letters that you have from the late Dr. Djindjic and from Mr. Svilanovic in the first annex to the provisional release motion. Can I respectfully refer the Chamber to those letters. Dealing first of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which annex?

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: It's annex 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Annex 1. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Dealing with the letter from Dr. Djindjic dated the 14th of January of this year, going to the second paragraph, what Dr. Djindjic said was this: "As president of Serbia, Mr. Milutinovic contributed to an orderly democratic transition, and for that reason, it was important for democratic stability that he served his full mandate as president. Also, Mr. Milutinovic is the first president of Serbia who orderly stepped down when his mandate expired. Immediately afterwards, Mr. Milutinovic has been ready to appear before the International Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Tribunal. For these reasons, one should consider that his appearance before the Court has been timely. In addition, Mr. Milutinovic cooperated fully with the federal government and the government of the Republic of Serbia on the issue of his coming to The Hague." And the Chamber will also be aware, I hope you've received these, of letters which are dated the 29th of April of this year. One of them signed by Mr. Zoran Zivkovic, who is Dr. Djindjic's successor as prime minister of Serbia, and another letter from Mr. Svilanovic. Can I just check that the Chamber has those?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have we got them? Just remind me, where are they? I suspect they are in the system somewhere, Mr. Livingston. My colleagues appear to have got it. I don't. Yeah, I have a copy now. Yes, we have them now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: I'm grateful. Dealing with the letter from Mr. Zivkovic, he, too, reiterates the fact that Mr. Milutinovic surrendered voluntarily to the International Criminal Tribunal, and he says: "I would like to inform you and the Trial Chamber that the guarantee of the government of the Republic of Serbia of 20th January, 2003, continues to be valid. The same applies to the views expressed in the letters of the late president of the government, Dr. Zoran Djindjic, dated the 14th and 20th of January, 2003 respectively." I'll come back to the last paragraph of that letter later. And the letter from Mr. Svilanovic of the same date is in not dissimilar terms to that which he had written earlier, but he does confirm that even after the abolition of the federation, that he would like to inform you that the guarantee of the government of the then Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, now Serbian Montenegro of 27th January continues to be valid. But the first point for present purposes is that all three of those people are telling you that this was a voluntary surrender. It's also completely different from that which one can perceive with the other two codefendants, because what seems to have been accepted as far as they were concerned is that they responded speedily to the passing or the passage of the law on cooperation with the Tribunal within a matter of two or three weeks. The Appeals Chamber was of the view that their backs were to the wall. They couldn't remain in Serbia securely any longer. They had no alternative but to go. What Mr. Svilanovic and Dr. Djindjic are saying puts this appellant, this defendant, in a completely different category. What they're saying is this: That on the fall of the Milosevic government in October 2000, he was crucial to the continued stability of the country. He was responsible for persuading Mr. Milosevic to step down. He called the new election speedily, and it is their view - and I read the passage from Dr. Djindjic's letter which Mr. Zivkovic agrees with - that it was important for the country that he served his full mandate as president which of course expired on the 29th of December last year. Now, that is a very different state of affairs from that which applies to the codefendants. Let me say immediately, because I don't want to be misunderstood on this, I'm not suggesting for a minute that legally that provides an answer. But as Judge Hunt pointed out in his dissenting judgement in the Ojdanic and Sainovic appeal case, what actually matters for provisional release purposes is not the provisions of Article 29 of the statute; what matters is the state of mind of this appellant -- this defendant. And in my submission, there is nothing to indicate that it wasn't this defendant's intention to go once this necessary and important role had been fulfilled in serving his country to the end of his mandate as its president. And I would submit that once his mandate was over, he came to this Tribunal reasonably promptly, and he can't be criticised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The fulfilment of that role of public service to his country, takes precedence over his answering the charges in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: No. I hope I've made myself clear. I don't pretend to say that if one looks at it in a strictly legal way that that explanation provides an answer to him not surrendering. Of course, he could have surrendered. It's physically possible for him to do so. But it is quite plain that his country needed him, needed him at the time of the fall of the Milosevic government. The politicians are telling you that it was important for continuity and for the stability of the state that he remained. And you know that now that once that particular matter is out of the way, his mandate is at an end, he has come to this Tribunal. So it's not a question -- Judge Shahabuddeen in the passage -- in his additional opinion in the Ojdanic and Sainovic appeal made it quite clear -- if you just bear with me, I'll just get the passage. Yes, what he said was this, at paragraph 10 of his additional judgement. He said that "Whatever explanation they might give, it was of their own will that they did not wish to surrender. That is what on the evidence the accused have to be understood to be accepting." That was in relation to certain statements that they had made on previous occasions within a short time before surrendering. Now, that is not the case with this appellant. He has an explanation. It is not a question in that same way of not wanting to come. There was an explanation. I'm not saying that strictly speaking in law he should have surrendered. Of course that's right in law, but the point is being made that that shouldn't be held against him in the context of provisional release where what matters is his state of mind. Did he intend to go to the Tribunal? Did he go voluntarily? And in my submission, if you accept the view of those politicians who are at the highest level of Serbian and union politics, then - as in my submission, you should do - there is a good explanation as to why he did not go before the end of his mandate. And I would add simply this: That I submitted earlier, and I repeat in open session, the passage from the B92 internet site quoting Peter Scheider, who is the president of the parliamentary assembly of the council of Europe, that one must have regard to the political and security risks which Serbia and indeed any country it may be subject to from time to time. And in my submission, one should not apply the law in such a way as to endanger the stability of the country. And what Dr. Djindjic, Mr. Svilanovic, and Mr. Zivkovic are all saying to you is this: That had Mr. Milutinovic strictly by the law surrendered to this Tribunal earlier, that would have endangered the stability of the country at a crucial time. That is their view. And I reiterate the point which is made in the pleadings, that none of us as lawyers, and I say that with the greatest respect to the Chamber, none of us as lawyers should lightly substitute our view for that of the politicians who were on the spot in the situation which they faced in October 2000. Your Honour, I'll deal briefly with the period pre October 2000. That's a matter as Your Honour knows I've already dealt with in private session. And I reiterate all the submissions that I made in private session concerning the pre-October 2000 period. Again, the matter is touched on in the pleadings, in paragraph 8 of the reply. And, Your Honour, the Chamber is aware of the security concerns which Mr. Milutinovic had at that time. That is, before October 2000. Your Honour, I repeat: I rely on all the submissions I made about that particular period before October 2000. And as far as the period after October 2000, I rely on the matters which are raised in the letters by the highly responsible politicians whose letters you have in front of you. And I rely on the statement by Peter Scheider that there are other concerns, other than a strict appliance of the law, which may excuse or may explain a failure to comply strictly with the international law requirements. Another part of the voluntary surrender situation or picture is this: That it appeared in the Ojdanic and Sainovic case that there were a number of statements which had been made to the press by both those gentlemen indicating a lack of willingness to come to the Tribunal for trial. That was what the Appeals Chamber accepted. The Prosecution don't make that point in relation to Mr. Milutinovic. And can I refer you in that context to their response at paragraph 9. What they say in paragraph 9, if you have it, is that the accused also relies in particular on his own contention that he's never made any statements to the effect that he would not surrender voluntarily to the Tribunal. While the accused may have more recently told the media that he would not resist transfer to the Tribunal or that he would surrender voluntarily, that has not been his consistent position since the issuance of the original indictment as reflected in media reports. Now, let me make it quite clear immediately that Mr. Milutinovic does not accept that he has been correctly quoted at any time as indicating that he did not have an intention to surrender to the Tribunal. But I don't particularly want to go down the path of disputing early reports. There are two referred to in the footnotes there. You can see 16 and 17, both of which are in January of 2001. There's also a statement by Vojislav Seselj which is referred to. And again, in my submission, there are good reasons to doubt the objectivity of such a statement. Seselj is clearly a political opponent of Mr. Milutinovic. He stood against him. He was the failed challenger for the post of president in 1997. And I would reiterate the point that I've made in the reply pleading. Do the Prosecution always rely on the truth of what Dr. Seselj says? One suspects not. And the most obvious example is that presumably by pleading not guilty to the indictment in his case, the Prosecution don't accept that he's being truthful. In my submission, one should be careful about accepting anything that he says, in particular one should be careful about accepting his point that if Mr. Milutinovic had really surrendered voluntarily, he would have got on a public plane and gone. That may be the way that Vojislav Seselj would go about things, hold a party the night before, get all his friends and relatives at the airport, fly off publicly. That's the way everybody would do it. This Chamber might think that other accused like this defendant might well have concerns for the privacy of their family. The essential thing is surrendering to the Tribunal, not how you do it, whether it's done in a conservative way or in a flamboyant way. But the important point is this: It's the acceptance by the Prosecution in paragraph 9 that there are no recent reports indicating that he wouldn't -- that he would resist transfer or that he wouldn't surrender voluntarily. That's what it says in the substantive text in paragraph 9. In my submission, one should go for these purposes. Whatever may have been said on an earlier occasion, or may not have been said, it's his recent state of mind that matters. That was what was so critical against Ojdanic and Sainovic, that their statements were recent. In this defendant's case, the Prosecution accept that there aren't any parallel statements which can be attributed to Mr. Milutinovic. Can I just also make one last point. There is a reference to a more recent article in the paper Nacional. But I think it's quite apparent when one looks at that, that it's based on double hearsay. It's what somebody tells the newspaper about what Mr. Milutinovic is alleged to have told him. It's not the most reliable source. It's not accepted Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. by Mr. Milutinovic as being accurate. And it's out of line, not only with other statements made by him, and it's also well out of line with the statements made by Dr. Djindjic, Mr. Svilanovic, and as confirmed now, by Mr. Zivkovic. And I would invite you to the conclusion that there is nothing in statements made to the press or on television, nothing of that order, parallel with those statements made by Ojdanic and Sainovic which can be held against this defendant. So again, that is a further pointer to the genuineness of the voluntary surrender in this particular case. It may be appropriate at this point to deal with a different point. And that is the point which is contained in the Prosecution's reply when this Chamber asked for confirmation from them as to whether they actually opposed Mr. Milutinovic's provisional release or not. And Your Honour may recall the reply that's given. If you just bear with me while I dig it out. It's paragraph 5 of that document. And it says as follows: "The Prosecution notes that its position regarding provisional release for Milutinovic, as with that for any accused seeking provisional release, might at some point in the future be subject to change should there be an appropriate material change in relevant circumstances. This might, for example, be the case, again a consideration that would be applicable to any accused seeking provisional release, should Mr. Milutinovic decide to cooperate with the Prosecution in a full and completely honest and forthcoming manner." The first point I make about that is this: That cooperation, let alone substantial cooperation, nowhere features in the text of Rule 65.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, now, Mr. Livingston, this argument was run I think in front of us in Ojdanic, and finds no favour with this Trial Chamber. The argument as to cooperation of course relates to totally different matters, and not necessarily this matter of provisional release. Although, of course, if the Prosecution want to state a view, they always can, but if you're going to argue that absence of cooperation shouldn't be held against him, I think you're pushing at an open door.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: I'm very grateful for that indication. I was simply going to say, because I do think it's an important point, and I make the point very briefly, that looking at that wording, and it's reiterated by the Prosecution in a later document which the Chamber will be aware of when they're replying to the Ojdanic Defence who replied to this document, that it's almost - and I say this with great respect to the Prosecution - it's almost an inducement to an accused to confess because what they're actually saying is this: We might take a different view completely on provisional release if this defendant gives a full and completely honest and forthcoming account of his role in the matters which are the subject of the trial. Now coming from the Prosecution, that must mean either a whole -- total confession, or a substantial confession to the indictment. In my submission, it is wholly wrong, wholly wrong, for the Prosecution to have a policy, and it sounds as though it's a policy, to try and induce such statements from a defendant. Your Honour will be very well aware, and I hesitate to make such a trite point to this Bench, but Your Honour particularly will be aware of the provisions in English law concerning Section 76 of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act which concerns confessions obtained as a result of things said or done, in that case, obviously by the police. Here it's the Prosecution who are suggesting if you are cooperative, if you're honest, and basically confess, then we might take a different view on provisional release. In my submission, that's a wholly improper submission for them to make. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think as a Presiding Judge has indicated, we have already taken a particular view on this. And I think it's a view shared by the European Court of Human Rights, that provisional release should not be used as a punishment. And I think, if I'm not mistaken, the Appeals Chamber, or at any rate, I think Judge Hunt also disapproved very strongly of that line of approach from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I respectfully agree. The problem is that the Prosecution continue to argue this point, and they have done it in this particular case not once but twice. But in my submission, the question of cooperation is irrelevant. I just say in passing on that, my client is in a completely different position to -- for example, Mr. Sainovic, who at the time of his application had not been interviewed at all. My client, as you know, was voluntarily interviewed by the Prosecution in Belgrade well before he even came to this Tribunal. The question of the veracity or otherwise of that interview is a matter which is doubtless this Trial Chamber will have to determine in due course. But he did agree to be interviewed. And in my submission, it's a matter that should be left to rest until trial, and it should play no part in the decision on this particular motion. Can I turn now to the issue of guarantees. The Prosecution say quite frankly that they don't accept the guarantees of the Serbian and what was the federal government in this case. In my submission, there may now be reason to review that position. Your Honours have the letters from Svilanovic and from Zoran Zivkovic. In particular, Mr. Zivkovic says: "I would also like to use this opportunity to reiterate the commitment of the government of the Republic of Serbia to cooperate with the International Criminal Tribunal." And Mr. Svilanovic has also made similar statements. The Prosecutor herself - I don't think there's any doubt about this - has also indicated publicly shortly after the murder of Dr. Djindjic that she was happy to note the positive attitude to the Tribunal both of the new union president and of the new prime minister of Serbia. Now, in my submission, if that is the Prosecution's position now, then the guarantees are worth the paper they're written on, and not, as the Prosecution have maintained to date in their response. And I would reiterate again the point made by Peter Scheider, the parliamentary president of the council of Europe, that it is essential to have regard to the political and security context in which any government makes its decisions. This government is indicating that it will do everything in its power to cooperate with the Tribunal. And that, of course, would involve ultimately in this defendant's case enforcing the guarantee if that's what it came to. But in my submission, one can properly ask with this defendant, is it really a case where we need a guarantee at all? Does he not, in fact, fall into the category which the Prosecution refer to in paragraph 12 of their response submissions, is he not in other words a person who's conduct has been exemplary or where his personal circumstances as such where no reliable guarantee is required. And if you are of the view that his surrender was voluntary, then in my submission, there is very little basis for saying that his behaviour isn't exemplary. And certainly, if one looks at his personal circumstances, in my submission, one can regard him as a highly reliable individual. You have annexed the provisional release motion, a curriculum vitae relating to Mr. Milutinovic. What that curriculum vitae indicates is this: That he's a law student, graduated in law in 1965. He became a member of the federal parliament in 1969. And I'm told by him, and I'm sure it's right, that he was the youngest member of parliament that there ever has been in the history of the country. He's director of the national library, an ambassador to Greece, federal minister for foreign affairs before he became president. In other words, a man who has given himself substantially to public service over many years, a law-abiding man. And I would remind you respectfully of what Zoran Djindjic said in his letter in annex 1, that he exercised his powers as president of Serbia in a lawful manner at all times and handed over the presidency for the first time in the history of the country in a lawful manner. This is a man who was brought up to respect the law. And he's a professional man. And he's a man of real substance. And as he reminds me, his name has featured for many years now in the international edition of who's who. He's a recognised international figure with weight and substance. And in my submission, the question of guarantees with such a man, with such a record, and such a reputation, in my submission, scarcely needs to be backed up with a guarantee. But the guarantees are there, and in my submission, they are worth the paper they are written on and you can rely on the word of those that give them. Your Honour, can I now turn -- perhaps I can just deal also before leaving that topic with the personal guarantee which he gives, which is also annexed to the provisional release motion. In my submission, again, bearing in mind the character of the accused, of the defendant with whom you are dealing, his personal guarantee that he will return to this Court, that he will abide by the orders of this Court is one which this Chamber can readily accept. Maybe with a person without his history and background and record, one couldn't make that point. But with this defendant in my submission, it's something that stands out from his very impressive curriculum vitae. Can I just reiterate that in the bundle...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Can I just reiterate that in the bundle which I handed up to the Chamber at the beginning of this afternoon's proceedings, at page 5, there is an extract from the ICTY weekly press briefing of the 21st of March. And the Prosecutor's spokesman, Ms. Hartman is quoted in the passage that I have marked as saying that it was those who killed Prime Minister Djindjic were wrong in believing that this might diminish the determination to continue the reform of the country to move forward and to cooperate with the Tribunal. She added that for the moment it was a good sign, both the president of the union and the new prime minister of Serbia were unequivocal in their support of the Tribunal. It's a point which in my submission adds considerable substance to the position on guarantees. Can I now turn to the next point, which is the high authority point in relation to this defendant. The fact that a defendant or an accused has or has perceived to have a high public profile has not of course proved a bar intrinsically to provisional release being granted. And to see that, one only has to look at such figures as Mrs. Plavsic, Sefer Halilovic, Rahim Ademi, and Admiral Jokic. Those are all high-ranking military or political figures who have been granted provisional release so it's not intrinsically a bar. The point about high authority, of course as the Chamber will be well aware, is really two fold: Firstly that the more important person that you are, the more serious the crimes that you may be found to have committed, and therefore the more serious the penalty that you will suffer, and therefore it is said the more reason you have not to appear at Court. The second point, of course, is that -- and this really arose first of all in the Brdjanin provisional release motion, and it was also dealt with in the Ojdanic and Sainovic appeal. The second point about high authority is that it's thought that if somebody of such status is released, it may provide the government of the country with a reason for not handing the person over because he's in receipt of -- or he has in his knowledge matters which could convict other people or put the country in a bad light. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. My primary submission about that is this: And I say so with the greatest respect. That Your Honour and Judge Robinson dealt with this issue of higher authority in the judgement in the Kordic and Cerkez case, and you'll find at the back of that little bundle I've handed you, there are a couple of pages that I've extracted for convenience from that judgement. The point really that I make here about Mr. Milutinovic is that while he may have a perceived high profile, his position really is much more symbol rather than substance. The first paragraph which has relevance to this case, and can I indicate this, it may be that these two paragraphs - it's 415 and 424 - it may be that those are the subject of appeal in the Kordic and Cerkez case. I know not. But Your Honour may be aware and will doubtless be pleased to know that these two paragraphs have been given substantial approval by no less a person than the former president Professor Antonio Cassese in his recently published book "International criminal law." What paragraph 415 says is this: "It follows that a government official will only be held liable under the doctrine of command responsibility if he was part of a superior subordinate relationship, even if that relationship is an indirect one, even though arguably, effective control may be achieved through substantial influence, a demonstration of such powers of influence will not be sufficient in the absence of a showing that he had effective control over subordinates in the sense of possessing the material ability to prevent subordinate offences or punish subordinate offenders after the commission of the crimes." And then an example, which is perhaps not relevant to this case is given. But over the page, paragraph 424, the Chamber said this: "A superior status when not clearly spelled out in an appointment order may be deduced from an analysis of the actual tasks performed by the accused in question. Evidence that an accused is perceived as having a high public profile manifested through public appearances and statements, and thus is exercising some authority, may be relevant to the overall assessment of his actual authority although not sufficient in itself to establish it without evidence of the accused's overall behaviour towards subordinates and his duties. Similarly the participation of an accused in high profile international negotiations would not be necessary in itself to demonstrate superior authority." Now, I wouldn't normally trespass in a motion of this sort on matters of evidence. But there are two matters of evidence which I just very briefly refer to, and I've got copies of those documents for the court. Perhaps with the usher's assistance, I could hand those out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, without knowing beforehand what the -- my learned colleague intends to -- what document he intends to refer to, the Prosecution would simply question whether this is the appropriate time or forum to discuss these matters of evidence going to substantive areas of liability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think we have to wait to hear what use he makes of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Well, it relates to this issue of whether this appellant is really symbol or substance. The first document in that bundle is a statement from a witness from whom this Chamber has already heard in the Milosevic trial. It's -- he's known in the trial as Radomir Tanic, and he, as I understood it, was a witness whom the Prosecution placed substantial reliance on. I've extracted page 3 simply from that statement, and you can see what he says there about Mr. Milutinovic. He says this: "I also reported to Milan Milutinovic, the president of Serbia, even though he did not have any decision-making power independent of Milosevic. My assessment of Milutinovic is that he was tolerated as being necessary for the de jure structure, however de facto Slobodan Milosevic was running Serbia as well as Yugoslavia." Now, the Prosecution put their case in terms of high authority on two grounds: Firstly, as the president of Serbia; and secondly, as a member of the supreme defence counsel of the former Yugoslavia. In my submission, that's an important Prosecution witness who supports the Defence point that Mr. Milutinovic was a figure of symbol rather than substance. The following document is an extract from the US department of State report on Serbia and Montenegro for the year 1999, which of course is the year of the war and it's the year in question in this case. And again, I've extracted the relevant part, it's the second page and you can see I hope the second main paragraph on the second page, starting "As a key of his hold on power." Does the Chamber have that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We do. But I really doubt very much if it's going to assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Well, the only point I wanted to make is one sentence. It says this: "Milosevic, effectively has destroyed the constitutional role of the supreme defence council essentially establishing himself as commander in chief of the Yugoslav army." Now it's this accused case, and I don't think there's any great secret about it, that destroyed the supreme defence council is a very apt word to have used because the supreme defence council while continuing to exist in form simply wasn't convened at all during the relevant period of the war. And that statement in my submission backs that up. And if you accept those two pieces of evidence, in my submission, they add weight to my proposition that this is not a defendant whose high authority is such that he should be regarded -- that it should be regarded as a bar to him being granted provisional release. Your Honour, I see that the clock is now just past 4.00. I have to say, I don't have a great deal more, but I haven't quite finished. But if Your Honour wishes to take the break now, it probably would be an appropriate moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll take the break now. Quarter of an hour, and we will sit until half past 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: I'm very grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If we can, we will finish this hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Livingston.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next point I want to deal with, I hope I can deal with quite shortly. And it's the second limb of Rule 65(B), that is, dealing with -- does the defendant pose a danger to any victim, witness, or other person. My point about that is essentially the same as in the pleadings, which is this: That this defendant was, of course, in Serbia for some time before he came here. There's never been any attempt to interfere with witnesses in the past, any suggestion that he's going to interfere with witnesses is in my submission pure speculation, and there is absolutely no evidence to support it whatsoever. I go further and invoke in this context again the outstanding reputation for integrity and public service which this defendant has demonstrated in the past. This does not mark him out as a man who is likely to try and manipulate his trial by interfering with victims, witnesses, or any other person. Your Honour, I hope that deals satisfactorily with that second objection. Before I turn to the topic of health, can I just deal with the other aspect of Rule 65(B) which is, if you like, the discretionary aspect, because the provision starts by saying "Release may be ordered by a Trial Chamber" if it's satisfied about the two criteria which I've been dealing with to date. The Prosecution deal with that point starting at paragraph 20 of their response brief. And essentially, the point in my submission is about the maintenance of confidence in the administration of justice by the Tribunal. My submission is far from damaging the confidence of administration of justice by the Tribunal, the release of this defendant would actually enhance the confidence that the public internationally would have in the administration of justice by this Tribunal. Dealing firstly with Serbia and Montenegro, Your Honour has the letters from Dr. Djindjic, Mr. Svilanovic, and from Mr. Zivkovic, and they deal with an important point here. It's annex 1 to the original motion. What Mr. Djindjic says in his letter of the 14th of January, 2003, is this: That "Mr. Milutinovic is coming back to Belgrade after his initial appearance in The Hague would certainly improve the image of the International Tribunal in Serbia, which in turn would contribute to efforts of my government to put at the disposal of the Tribunal other indicted individuals that may be in Serbia." And it's a point reiterated by Mr. Svilanovic. I don't think I need to read any particular passages from his letters. The Court has them. And Mr. Zivkovic adopts the comments made by Dr. Djindjic and reiterates his commitment to the Tribunal. So in my submission, in terms of the public in Serbia and the issue of confidence in the administration of justice in Serbia, there is very much to be said for this -- for the provisional release of this defendant. And it is -- would be helpful for them to see that a defendant doesn't necessarily, even if he may be perceived to have a high profile, have to remain in custody for probably a lengthy period of time before his trial. And that this Tribunal is prepared to be fair to Serbs and where it is appropriate and where Rule 65 is satisfied, to grant the provisional release of the defendant. The second aspect of my submission on this point is contained in annex 1 to the reply to the Prosecutor's response. And what that contains is a number of comments by international dignitaries at the time of Mr. Milutinovic's surrender. The Chamber can read them for themselves. But what essentially they come to is that a number of international dignitaries congratulate and indeed welcome Mr. Milutinovic's surrender voluntarily to this Tribunal. In my submission, granted that that is the case, this is hardly a situation where people internationally are going to sit up and say "How can the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia conscientiously release Mr. Milutinovic?" He surrendered voluntarily, and his behaviour is commended and welcomed. And in my submission, he ought and indeed his behaviour is such to indicate that provisional release is appropriate in the circumstances of his behaviour and of his surrender and of all the circumstances which I've already dealt with. So internationally in terms of boosting confidence in the administration of justice, the pointers in my submission are towards provisional release in this case. Your Honour, that's what I say about the discretionary aspect. One final point before I turn to the issue of health: Mr. Milutinovic is anxious that I remind the Chamber of a point which I'm sure it is aware of, and that is simply this: That there is no longer any state of emergency in Serbia. So if there were any concerns about returning this defendant to a country which -- where the control of the government might in any way have been in any doubt at all, that is gone. Law and order has been maintained. The government is in full control, a government which is favourable towards this Tribunal. Your Honour, turning to the health issue, I'm going to call Mr. Milutinovic in one moment. Can I just deal with that issue in this way: The Chamber has a number of medical reports in this case starting Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. with that of Mr. Milasinovic, it is at annex 4 to the original provisional release motion. And without going into any of the details of his medical condition, if one looks particularly at the report which -- the most recent report, that is the 10th of January, 2003, what is apparent from that report in my submission is this: That there will be periods of time when Mr. Milutinovic's health is good. As good as it can be for somebody with the history of serious heart surgery that he has. In particular, what Mr. Milasinovic says in the first paragraph of that report is: "Last time I saw him during the summer," and he refers to a medical report of August the 10th, 2002, "he had no anginal symptoms at that time." So it is a feature, it would seem, of this accused's medical history that sometimes he may be symptom-free, but sometimes as Mr. Milasinovic says in the last paragraph of his report, he can be at elevated risk of sudden cardiac death. And in my submission, none of those conclusions are actually fundamentally at odds with what has been found by Mr. Van der Sloot. The Chamber will of course have those reports. There are two reports which in my submission one must have regard to. The first one is that dated the 11th of March, 2003, which in a sense was a provisional report. And the second one is that dated the 14th of April, 2003. Just dealing briefly with the 11th of March report first of all, he talks -- the term he uses at intervals during that report is of premature ventricular contractions which he shortens to PVCs. Perhaps, I can for convenience use that contraction. And he does indicate in that report that a patient - this is in the fourth paragraph - a patient with frequent PVCs, that is, three or more in a row, may have -- or he says there is in fact a higher risk of sudden cardiac death. Now that is a very similar conclusion to that which Mr. Milasinovic had indicated in the report which I've referred to a few moments ago. In the letter -- it's a letter but it's also a report of the 14th of April, in paragraph 2 of that letter, he says this: "There was made a 24-hour ECG, showed frequent ventricular ectopy." Now, I stress I'm not a medical expert, but my understanding of that phrase is that it means much the same as frequent PVCs. In other words, runs of PVCs. He goes on to say, being multiform PVCs. He of course concludes that at the moment, and I do stress that that last sentence which is over the page in that report simply says that he has no real cardiac complaints at the moment which justify the conclusion that his clinical cardiac condition at this moment is acceptable. It offers no prognosis as to the future. And in my submission, it's not actually out of line with what Mr. Milasinovic is saying, that there are periods fortunately and happily where this defendant -- where his cardiac condition may be acceptable. But equally, Mr. Milasinovic is indicating that his history shows that there are going to be other periods, particularly when he has these frequent PVCs, when his heart condition may present this elevated risk of cardiac arrest. And in my submission, one cannot rule that out in this particular case. Let me say straight away, and Mr. Milutinovic would urge me to make this point very clear, that he doesn't doubt the expertise of the doctors in Holland. He doesn't doubt the excellence of the hospitals. Indeed, I think from what he's experienced himself, he's impressed. But the question in his mind, and he will deal with this in a moment himself, the question very much in his mind is if he reaches a stage, as he may, where there is an elevated risk of cardiac arrest, what is going to happen then? Because it is quite apparent that particularly over weekends, bank holidays, any time from 5.00 Friday afternoon onwards, there is very limited staffing in the UN Detention Unit and the potential to react quickly to an emergency such as might be presented, in my submission this is not a criticism of the Detention Unit in any way, is limited, and one must be cautious to expose him to any risk which one -- which might foreseeably occur and which his history indicates. And in my submission, looking at the Milasinovic report, that risk is a real one. At the moment, the heart condition is acceptable. But one cannot by any means guarantee on the documentation that you have that will always be the case. And in my submission, granted that it's now accepted decision in Mrksic, it indicates that, that the health of a defendant is a relevant factor to be taken into account for provisional release purposes. There can be really no question that from the health point of view this defendant would be better served if he wasn't in custody where there is a -- he's easier to react to emergencies and where, to put it frankly, and I hope in a sense this is readily acceptable, where there is less stress. There is inevitable stress involved in being in custody facing the sort of allegations which this defendant does. And in my submission, there will clearly as a matter of common sense be much less stress if he's able to be at home with his family and friends and to prepare his case in familiar surroundings. So in my submission, at the end of the day, the evidence about the health, while mercifully from his point of view hopeful and optimistic at the moment does not indicate that provisional release on that ground would be an inappropriate step. Your Honour, I've taken a long time, I'm sorry about that. But this is a very important motion from Mr. Milutinovic's point of view. Can I call him to address you as he wishes to on the medical matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll go into private session. There's a matter that Judge Robinson wants to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Caric.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Let me present the explanation of guarantees by reading the original text in Serbian, B/C/S. Thank you very much. [Interpretation] Your Honours, on behalf of the state union of Serbia and Montenegro, it is my honour that I'm able to address this Trial Chamber today. Following the application of the accused Milan Milutinovic for provisional release with protective measures, the government of Serbia and Montenegro fully abides by the guarantees given by the federal government on its 25th session held on the 23rd of January, 2003. It means that the government of Serbia and Montenegro are still proposing that the accused, Mr. Milan Milutinovic, the former president of the Republic of Serbia be provisionally released and hereby undertakes that should the Trial Chamber grant the provisional release of the accused and to allow him to stay in the territory of Serbia and Montenegro during that period of time, will respect all orders of the Trial Chamber so that he can appear before the Trial Chamber when required to do so. This includes all previous undertakings, obligations, and regarding the travel of Mr. Milutinovic, the control of his stay on the territory of Serbia and Montenegro, and the regular informing of the Tribunal of the situation, including the respect of protective measures. This has been given in accordance with Article 26 of the law on cooperation with the Tribunal, which applies only to the persons who have voluntarily surrendered to the Tribunal. The government of Serbia and Montenegro consider that Mr. Milutinovic has surrendered himself voluntarily although the indictment was confirmed on the 24th of May, 1999, Mr. Milutinovic has remained in his office as the president of the Republic of Serbia until the expiration of his mandate which took place on the 29th of December, 2002. Following the political changes in Serbia in October 2000, this was very important for the political stability of the country itself and the entire region. Immediately after the expiration of the mandate of Mr. Milutinovic, he expressed his willingness to surrender voluntarily to the Tribunal. Immediately after the expiration of the mandate -- of his mandate, Mr. Milutinovic expressed his readiness to surrender voluntarily to the Tribunal. And until his arrival in The Hague, he was in contact both with the government of the Republic of Serbia and the ministry of foreign affairs of Serbia and Montenegro. As well as the Office of the Prosecutor in Belgrade. He never went into hiding, and his decision to surrender voluntarily, although it was conditioned by the development of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the democratic changes taking place in Serbia, was only his. Mr. Milutinovic did not appear before this Tribunal under any kind of constraint or pressure. The voluntary surrender of Mr. Milutinovic, the former president of the Republic of Serbia, constitutes a very strong incentive to other individuals to do the same, to undertake the same step. And a positive ruling of the Chamber pursuant to this motion would further contribute to this. For the above-mentioned reasons, the minister of foreign affairs of Serbia and Montenegro, Mr. Goran Svilanovic, decided to address the President of the Tribunal with a letter in order to provide further support to the guarantee which was offered by the federal government. The president of the government of Serbia, the late Mr. Zoran Djindjic, acted in a similar fashion. In a letter sent to the chief prosecutor of the Tribunal, he made his contribution to the guarantees offered by his government. This was further confirmed several days ago in the letters by the president of the government of Republic of Serbia, Mr. Zivkovic, and by Mr. Svilanovic, minister of foreign affairs. Your Honours, the provisional release of Mr. Milan Milutinovic pending trial with the application of relevant protective measures in our view would not pose any risk to the further successful conduct of this case. This can be concluded on the basis of the seriousness with which our government has so far fulfilled its obligations. As part of the process of establishing a full cooperation with this Tribunal, with the Prosecution and the Defence counsel, we believe that this process is constantly being promoted. Serbia and Montenegro have so far surrendered six individuals to this Tribunal, including a former head of state, the former president. A large number of indictees have surrendered voluntarily, encouraged by the campaign of our government. Serbia and Montenegro are ready -- are willing to continue with the arrests of all indictees who find themselves on the territory of these two countries. The cooperation with respect to finding the accused and also with respect of the waiver of their obligation to keep state secrets is also going very well, and the requests of the Prosecutor pursuant to Rule 54 bis have also been adequately processed, and the cooperation with that respect is also going well. As for the request of the Prosecutor pursuant to Rule 54 bis, this request has been mentioned by the Prosecutor as an argument for their allegations in their response to the motion of the accused for provisional release of the 6th of February. With regard to this, I wish to emphasise that the request of the Prosecutor pursuant to Rule 54 bis is not relevant for the current arguments because it is a direct litigation between the Office of the Prosecutor and Serbia and Montenegro which cannot in any way affect the position of the accused in the arguments for his motion of provisional release. The fight against organised crime which, after the assassination of the Serb prime minister Zoran Djindjic has yielded excellent results, has also contributed to the strengthening of democratic stability in our country. And therefore, creation of even better conditions for all forms of cooperation with this Tribunal. Serbia and Montenegro wish to refute the arguments offered by the Prosecutor in paragraphs 12 to 15 of their response of the 6th of February. We wish to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to the unacceptable character of the allegations made therein; in particular, in paragraph 14 of their response whereby they have cast doubt to the reliability of the guarantees offered by Serbia and Montenegro. In future, as stated by the Prosecutor, when current officials are no longer in power, in all cases in which the Court has so far accepted the guarantees offered by our government, namely, the case of Biljana Plavsic, Pavle Strugar, Miodrag Jokic, Momcilo Gruban, and Momir Talic, the surveillance hasn't so far encountered any particular difficulties. All persons who are currently under surveillance have regularly responded to the summons of Trial Chambers, and not a single party to the proceedings held before the Tribunal has ever had any objection as to the conduct of the local authorities. Therefore, we expect that the Prosecutor treat the guarantees offered by Serbia and Montenegro with adequate amount of respect. At this point, Your Honours, this is all I have to say. I thank you very much for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I will -- given the time, I will make my best efforts to move along quickly, although I'm not sure that I will be able to finish prior to 5.30. The Prosecution will begin first by making some general points, taking into consideration in the course of those points the arguments raised here today by my learned colleague as well as the representative from the state that is now currently known as Serbia and Montenegro. Secondly, the Prosecution will turn to any other points that have not otherwise been addressed. My learned colleague has stated that at the bottom of this issue of provisional release is the issue -- the question of whether the surrender of the accused was voluntary or not. The Prosecution agrees that this was a very important element in the consideration of an application for provisional release. In this case, the Prosecution notes that the accused has been a fugitive for nearly four years. I believe the actual time period is somewhere in the neighbourhood of three years and eight months. During this time period, the accused could at any time have surrendered. The Prosecution submits, and his allegations to the contrary will be addressed later in these submissions. The original indictment was issued in May of 1999 and was a matter of international news. The accused does not and in fact could not deny that he was in any way unaware of this indictment. The Prosecution turns next to the conditions under which for nearly four years the accused was at large. The accused was openly enjoying the protection of his government. In fact, and indeed, in the past before this very Trial Chamber, a representative of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia has stated openly that the accused would not be transferred prior to the end of his term in office despite the fact that he had been indicted in May of 1999. The Prosecution submits that these circumstances show that the accused demonstrated by his actions what his attitude was towards the Tribunal. In short, that he did not respect the authority of the Tribunal, and that it was his intention to in the context of provisional release get away with as much as he could while he could enjoy the protection of the authorities in his country. In fact, the Prosecution submits that it was only when the accused had to surrender that he decided that he would. This calculation resulting in part on the passage of the law on cooperation, this is a point that perhaps we didn't make adequately in our response brief. And we would just point to Article 36 of the law on cooperation in that regard, which states that an accused who voluntarily surrenders shall receive guarantees for provisional release, and I emphasise that it states that he shall receive guarantees for provisional release. This law is publicly available, the Prosecution does have translations available if it would be of assistance to the Trial Chamber. I turn next to the issue of prior statements of the accused. In the Prosecution's filings, the Prosecution cites an article entitled "I will not face war crimes court - Serbian president" with the byline of the Reuters news agency. And dated on the 17th of January, 2001. And I'll read briefly -- very briefly from that article. The article states, and this is a quotation of the accused,

utterances.speaker: MR. MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: "I see no reason to surrender myself to the Tribunal. I think the verdict of my people is the main one, and these artificial creations," referring to the Tribunal, "for trying an entire people and its leadership is something I do not recognise." The accused is later in this same article quoted as saying, speaking to the interviewer: "You know yourself that The Hague Tribunal is a political court, and Kostunica has spoken his mind about that recently. He clearly said what he thought about it." Despite the allegations now raised that -- the argument now raised that the accuse did not say these words, the Prosecution submits that these words are consistent with the conduct -- conduct of the accused in avoiding the jurisdiction of this Tribunal for nearly four years and is properly reflective of his state of mind at that time. The accused points to recent changes in his statements where he states that now recognised the Tribunal. The Prosecution submits that it is not surprising that he should have changed his view. This is consistent with our argument that the accused recognised the Tribunal when he believed, and we emphasise that when he believed that after four years of living as a fugitive, his period of protection under stated authorities may be coming to an end and therefore chose to surrender to the Tribunal. The Prosecution in its filings also quoted a second article dated the 24th of December. This article entitled "Serbia's Milutinovic refuses to surrender to Hague Tribunal." And I'll quote just briefly from that as well. This article states: "Serbian President Milan Milutinovic has made to deal with the authorities and has no intention of surrendering to The Hague Tribunal. One of Milutinovic's close associates whom the president has asked to pass this message on to the media told Nacional," Nacional being the source of that article. The Prosecution submits is what this shows quite simply is the surrender of the accused was not voluntary surrender within the meaning and context of Rule 65 (B), and certainly in line of the jurisprudence of this rule. Under such circumstances, the Prosecution submits that the personal guarantees should be given little weight and cannot be a strong argument for release. On the jurisprudence, the Prosecution relies on the Appeals Chamber's decision on Sainovic and Ojdanic in June of last year. I'm sorry, I believe in October of last year. This decision, of course, offers relevant guidance on the issue of provisional release for this accused. The facts are very similar to this accused, and on those facts, the Appeals Chamber found that the surrender of the accused Sainovic and Ojdanic could not be considered voluntary. There is of course a difference between the facts of that case or the facts of those two applications and the facts of this application. In this case, the accused refused to surrender, and his refusal to surrender continued for nearly a year after his coaccused had surrendered to this Tribunal. This difference the Prosecution submits makes the grounds for detention even more compelling in this case. On the jurisprudence, the Prosecution would also refer the Trial Chamber to the Appeals Chamber decision in Mrksic which upheld denial of the application for provisional release of that accused. In that case, the Trial Chamber found that surrender after six years of refusing to surrender to the Tribunal could have only limited impact in favour of release. In fact, the Trial Chamber in that case stated that it was rather doubtful whether the accused having failed to voluntarily surrender during all those years can be treated as if, in fact, he had voluntarily surrendered. In that case as well, the Trial Chamber therefore held that it was not satisfied with the personal undertakings of the accused seeking provisional release. Both these findings of fact by the Trial Chamber were upheld by the Appeals Chamber in its decision. The Prosecution would also briefly refer to the Trial Chamber's decision in the Martic application for provisional release denying release. Similarly, the accused Martic had been a fugitive for approximately six years. And on those and other factors, the Trial Chamber found that he had not satisfied the Trial Chamber that he would return if required for trial -- or rather, when required for trial. The Martic decision certification for appeal on that case was not granted. The Prosecution will now turn to its second point. Allegations and arguments by the accused to the contrary, the Prosecution submits that there was no justification or excuse for failure to surrender during these four years. The Prosecution would note first that despite the arguments that the accused contributed to democratic transition in Serbia and Yugoslavia, or in some way contributed to political stability in those -- in that republic and that state should be given no weight. First of all, there is simply no support in the jurisprudence, nor in the statute or rules of the Tribunal, that such political considerations can justify defiance of the Tribunal's authority; rather, as the Prosecution has indicated in its submissions, the statute and the rules expressly exclude in several instances such types of considerations. And I refer the Trial Chamber again to Statute Article 7 (ii), and also to Rule 58 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Despite the clear exclusion of domestic considerations in the context of surrender and transfer as set out in the statute and the rules, the accused goes even one step further and asserts that such political considerations must not only be taken into consideration in this context, but furthermore, that the Trial Chamber must accept them as they come in at their face value and cannot second guess or question them. The Prosecution submits that this is tantamount to saying that this is essentially a non-justiciable question that the Trial Chamber must accept. We submit that the Trial Chamber should simply reject this further invitation to insert political considerations in the provisional release context. As we indicated in our filings, to do otherwise would create incentives to foment conditions that would in fact render surrender to the Tribunal a threat to political stability. The experience of this Tribunal from its early days, even to the present, in bringing indictees before it shows that this is no hypothetical concern, and certainly not an extreme one as suggested by the accused in his reply brief. The Prosecution would next point to paragraph 8 of the reply brief. In that paragraph, the accused asserts that he could not surrender before October 2000 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we'll deal with that in private session, if you want to make some submissions about that. How much longer do you think you're going to be, Mr. Shin?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do not feel that you've got to speed, because we may have to have another hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, I would anticipate chose to a half hour, perhaps more. There were quite a number of issues raised at some level in detail in the course of these lengthy proceedings, and I would request adequate time to treat those matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're considering a suitable time to adjourn to. Maybe the Registrar can assist us. Mr. Livingston, what's your position? Are you here tomorrow morning, for instance?

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Well, I have actually got a flight booked back this evening, but...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is your position tomorrow? Because there is a view that we should finish this off. I mean, you've got a flight.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are you elsewhere tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Not as far as I'm aware. But one never knows with barrister's clerks to what they may have done in the interim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Shin, does this make any difference to you when we hear this? The alternatives are that we hear it tomorrow morning, or that we put it off to another day. Does it make any difference to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm entirely at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Livingston, what would you ask us to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: May I just take some instructions on it in case Mr. Milutinovic has any particular views.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, we took a little bit longer than I thought. Mr. Milutinovic leaves it really in the Court's hands. I think if the Tribunal doesn't mind cancelling my flight and booking me another one tomorrow, I would be quite content to speak to my clerks and finish this matter tomorrow, if that suited the Chamber better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll sit tomorrow morning, 9.00. There will be half an hour for the Prosecution, ten minutes for a response. I take it that will be on the basis that your ticket is a matter for the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Excuse me, if I may, I indicated that the remainder may take a half hour or more, if it would be possible to have some additional time if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very little.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Caric, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARIC
utterances.text: I would be very grateful if the Trial Chamber allow me to be present for tomorrow's hearing because I would like to hear opinion of the Prosecutor in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, you could be present, of course. Most certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 5.34 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 2nd day of May, 2003 at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the motion hearing adjourned at
